The kernel returns the result as if the `else:` block were deleted. `break`/`continue` are accepted inside kernel loops (they lower to `T.break_loop()` / `T.continue_loop()`), so a loop `else:` — "run this after the loop finishes without a `break`" — has a well-defined meaning here; it is not a no-op construct. Minimal repro below: a loop stores `A[i]+1`, and its `else:` clause adds `100` to every element. The correct result is `A+1+100`; the actual result is `A+1` (the `else:` never runs). A control kernel with the `else:` body hand-inlined after the loop returns the correct values, confirming the values are computable and the discrepancy is the dropped `else:`, not a harness artifact. `while…else` behaves identically (collapsed below). Not a regression — see Provenance. ### Reproducible example code ```python import tilelang import tilelang.language as T import torch N = 8 @T.prim_func def with_forelse(A: T.Tensor((N,), "int32"), B: T.Tensor((N,), "int32")): with T.Kernel(1, threads=1): for i in T.serial(N): B[i] = A[i] + 1 else: # runs after the loop completes without break for j in T.serial(N): B[j] = B[j] + 100 @T.prim_func def control(A: T.Tensor((N,), "int32"), B: T.Tensor((N,), "int32")): with T.Kernel(1, threads=1): for i in T.serial(N): B[i] = A[i] + 1 for j in T.serial(N): # the else body, hand-inlined = the correct behavior B[j] = B[j] + 100 A = torch.arange(N, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda") ref = A + 1 + 100 # else runs -> +100 got = tilelang.compile(with_forelse, out_idx=[-1])(A) ctl = tilelang.compile(control, out_idx=[-1])(A) print("for...else:", got.cpu().tolist()) # -> [1, 2, ..., 8] (else dropped) print("control :", ctl.cpu().tolist()) # -> [101, 102, ..., 108] print("for...else correct?", torch.equal(got, ref)) # -> False print("control correct?", torch.equal(ctl, ref)) # -> True ```
while…else face — same root, same silent drop ```python @T.prim_func def while_else(A: T.Tensor((N,), "int32"), B: T.Tensor((N,), "int32")): with T.Kernel(1, threads=1): i = T.alloc_local((1,), "int32") i[0] = 0 while i[0] < N: B[i[0]] = A[i[0]] + 1 i[0] = i[0] + 1 else: for j in T.serial(N): B[j] = B[j] + 100 # expected [101..108]; got [1..8] -> while...else correct? False ```
### Traceback No traceback — the kernel compiles and runs to completion; the `else:` body is silently omitted and the result is deterministically wrong. ### Expected behavior The `else:` body should either be executed with Python's loop-`else` semantics (it runs when the loop is not exited by `break`), or, if the eager frontend does not intend to support it, the frontend should reject it with a clear error rather than silently drop it. The frontend already raises `NotImplementedError` for other syntax it does not handle (e.g. attribute-target assignment and unsupported `for` targets), so a clean diagnostic is consistent with its own convention. ### Additional context **Root cause.** The eager AST transform does not emit the `else:` clause of a loop: [`visit_For`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/6af825e072d305a87ac039be0abd27b83c9a1bdc/tilelang/language/eager/ast.py#L318) and [`visit_While`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/6af825e072d305a87ac039be0abd27b83c9a1bdc/tilelang/language/eager/ast.py#L482) only pass `node.body` into the rewritten frame and never reference `node.orelse`, so the `else:` statements are dropped during the source-to-source rewrite before any IR is built. By contrast [`visit_If`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/6af825e072d305a87ac039be0abd27b83c9a1bdc/tilelang/language/eager/ast.py#L291-L301) does thread `node.orelse` through, so the omission is specific to the two loop visitors.
Note on the break interaction (why "execute" is not a trivial fix) `break` lowers to a runtime `T.break_loop()`, so faithful `for…else` semantics (run the `else:` only if the loop finished without a `break`) require guarding the `else:` body on whether a break fired at runtime, not just appending it after the loop. In the common no-`break` case the `else:` body is unconditional and the hand-inlined control above shows it is directly computable; the general case needs the break-condition guard. Rejecting the clause with a clear error is the simpler alternative if full support is out of scope.
**Suggested fix.** `visit_For`/`visit_While` (`eager/ast.py`) should thread `node.orelse` through the rewrite the way `visit_If` already does — emitting the `else:` body with loop-`else` semantics (guarded on whether a `T.break_loop()` fired at runtime) — or, if full support is out of scope, raise a clear `NotImplementedError` for a loop with an `else:` clause rather than silently dropping it, matching the frontend's existing diagnostics for unsupported syntax. Full loop-`else` semantics is the substantial option; the `NotImplementedError` is small. **Provenance.** The eager AST frontend was introduced/relocated to `tilelang/language/eager/ast.py` no later than #1632 (2026-01-09); `visit_For`/`visit_While` have never emitted `node.orelse` in that file's history, so this is not a regression. **Dedup.** I searched the open and closed tracker and found no existing report of a dropped loop `else:` clause. **Reach.** The trigger is a Python `for…else` / `while…else` inside a kernel — it is the standard Python way to express "do X after the loop unless it exited early via `break`," and `break`/`continue` are accepted in kernel loops, so the construct is expressible and meaningful here. That said, loop `else:` is an obscure Python feature most users never write (and often do not know exists), so the trigger is rare in practice. It is not documented as supported by TileLang, and no shipped test exercises a loop `else:` inside a kernel, so nothing in-repo trips it. The silent drop affects any loop `else:` regardless of body contents. **Impact.** The trigger is narrow: it needs a loop `else:` clause written inside a kernel, an undocumented, untested construct that no shipped code exercises. But when it fires the failure is silent and deterministic — no error, and the entire `else:` body is dropped, so whatever it computes (here a +100 over the whole output region) simply never happens; the wrong result is the same on every run, so it can slip into a workload undetected. Fixing it either honors the construct's loop-`else` semantics or converts it into a clear compile-time rejection, closing a silent-miscompile hole in the eager frontend's handling of a valid Python control-flow form.

title: Silent all-zeros miscompilation of mamba-ssm's Mamba-3 MIMO kernel on GB10 (sm_121) — depends on JIT compile order, reproduces on 0.1.8 and 0.1.13
body:
## Environment

- GPU: NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark, sm_121), aarch64
- CUDA 13.0, torch 2.11.0+cu130, Python 3.12
- tilelang: reproduces on **0.1.8 and 0.1.13** (both from PyPI aarch64 wheels)
- Kernel: `mamba_ssm/ops/tilelang/mamba3/mamba3_mimo` (`mamba_mimo_fwd_kernel`), via
  mamba-ssm @ `e9594ce` (git main 2026-08-22)
- Model: official `state-spaces/mamba3-mimo-1.5b` (bf16, `mimo_rank: 4`)

## Summary

The compiled `mamba_mimo_fwd_kernel` produces **all-zero outputs** (downstream: logits
whose argmax is the "0" token forever) for a specific input shape — but **only when that
shape is the first kernel compiled in a fresh process**. The same shape compiled after
other shapes in the same process produces correct output. No error or warning is raised:
the kernel compiles "successfully" and silently returns zeros.

## Repro (fails: first compile in fresh process)

```python
import torch
from mamba_ssm.models.mixer_seq_simple import MambaLMHeadModel
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3-8B")
model = MambaLMHeadModel.from_pretrained(
    "state-spaces/mamba3-mimo-1.5b", device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16).eval()
prompt = ("Inventory record: the component serial number is CN-4821, rated 375 watts, "
          "installed 2024-11-03. The serial number of that component is")
ids = tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to("cuda")   # seqlen 35
with torch.inference_mode():
    for _ in range(4):
        ids = torch.cat([ids, model(ids).logits[:, -1].argmax(-1, keepdim=True)], dim=1)
print(tok.decode(ids[0][-4:]))   # -> " 0000"   (expected: " CN-4821…", which SISO produces)
```

Observed in 3 independent fresh-process runs (two on 0.1.8, one on 0.1.13):
output is `" 000000000…"` — the model deterministically emits the `0` token.

## Control (passes: same shape, compiled after others)

Sweeping seqlens 24→71 of the same text in one process (so seqlen 35 is compiled ~10th),
the seqlen-35 forward is **healthy**: logits std ≈ 2.0, argmax matches the SISO
checkpoint's, generation recalls "CN-4821" correctly. All 48 shapes in the sweep pass.
So the miscompilation is a function of JIT/compile-context state, not of the shape itself.

- Kernel logs in the failing runs show a normal `TileLang begins/completes to compile
  kernel 'mamba_mimo_fwd_kernel'` pair — nothing distinguishes the bad compile.
- The SISO checkpoint (triton path, no tilelang) is correct on identical inputs, ruling
  out weights/tokenizer/driver issues.

## Secondary pain point

Each new sequence length triggers a full ~7-8 s JIT recompile of
`mamba_mimo_fwd_kernel` (0.1.13 included — the executable reuse added there appears to
apply per-shape only). Token-by-token generation therefore costs ~8 s/token. If there is
a supported way to compile shape-generic / symbolic-seqlen kernels, a pointer would be
appreciated; otherwise consider this a feature request that would matter a lot for
autoregressive SSM decode.

Possibly related: #2201 (Mamba-3 MIMO on sm_120: shared-memory overflow, perf issues).
A companion issue on the mamba-ssm side (their Mamba-3 `step()` path) is filed at
state-spaces/mamba#1022 (https://github.com/state-spaces/mamba/issues/1022) — happy to cross-link, provide cache dumps, generated CUDA source
from good vs bad compiles, or run patches on this hardware.

title: [BUG][Fuzzer][wrong-code] `T.clamp` silently drops `NaN` and returns the `min` bound instead of propagating `NaN`
body:
### Required prerequisites

- [x] I have read the documentation <https://tilelang.com>.
- [x] I have searched the [Issue Tracker](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/issues) that this hasn't already been reported. (comment there if it has.)
- [x] I have tried the latest version of TileLang.

### What version of TileLang are you using?

0.1.13

### System information

NVIDIA L40S (sm_89), CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.13.0, Python 3.13. The behavior is architecture-independent — the wrong value comes from the CUDA `fminf`/`fmaxf` NaN semantics, which are identical on every NVIDIA target; only sm_89 was run.

### Problem description

`T.clamp(x, lo, hi)` on a `NaN` input silently returns `lo` (the lower bound) instead of `NaN`. The reference semantics `T.clamp` should match are **`torch.clamp` and `numpy.clip`, both of which propagate `NaN`** (verified this session) — these are the frameworks a TileLang kernel is written against and differentially tested against. The kernel compiles and runs to completion with no error, so the wrong value is silent.

Clamping is used in the shipped fp8-quantization examples (`T.clamp(y / y_s, fp8_min, fp8_max)` in `examples/cast/example_group_per_split_token_cast_to_fp8.py:48`, `example_per_token_cast_to_fp8.py:35`, and the DeepSeek act-quant examples), where a `NaN` in the input would be quantized to `fp8_min` rather than surfacing.

`T.clamp` lowers to `min(max(x, lo), hi)`; the emitted CUDA is `min(max(A[i], -1.0f), 1.0f)`. `NaN` fed to CUDA `max`/`min` (`fmaxf`/`fminf`) returns the non-`NaN` operand, so `max(NaN, -1.0f)` gives `-1.0f` and the `NaN` is gone before the outer `min` runs.

The same `NaN`-suppression is visible in `T.max`/`T.min` on their own (not just via `T.clamp`) — see the neighbor note below.

Not a regression: `clamp` has been `min(max(...))` since it was added.

### Reproducible example code

```python
import tilelang, tilelang.language as T, torch

N = 4

@T.prim_func
def main(A: T.Tensor((N,), "float32"), C: T.Tensor((N,), "float32")):
    with T.Kernel(1, threads=N) as bx:
        i = T.get_thread_binding()
        C[i] = T.clamp(A[i], T.float32(-1.0), T.float32(1.0))

kernel = tilelang.compile(main, out_idx=[1])

a   = torch.tensor([float('nan'), 2.0, 0.5, -5.0], dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
got = kernel(a).cpu()
ref = torch.clamp(a.cpu(), -1.0, 1.0)                 # trusted oracle
print("T.clamp :", got.tolist())                      # -> [-1.0, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0]  NaN -> -1.0 (min bound)
print("torch   :", ref.tolist())                      # -> [nan, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0]   NaN preserved
print("NaN preserved:", torch.isnan(got[0]).item())   # -> False  (should be True)

# control: with no NaN present, T.clamp matches torch exactly
b = torch.tensor([2.0, 0.5, -5.0, 0.0], dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
print("finite ctrl OK:", torch.equal(kernel(b).cpu(), torch.clamp(b.cpu(), -1.0, 1.0)))  # -> True
```

### Traceback

No traceback — the kernel compiles and runs to completion; the result is silently wrong and deterministic.

### Expected behavior

`T.clamp(NaN, lo, hi)` returns `NaN`.

The reference semantics that matter most here are **`torch.clamp` and `numpy.clip`** — both propagate `NaN` (a `NaN` input yields a `NaN` output; verified this session on 0.1.13's PyTorch and NumPy). These are the libraries TileLang kernels are written against and validated against, so `T.clamp` diverging from them on `NaN` is the core defect. The finite-input control already matches `torch` exactly, so only a `NaN` operand disagrees.

This also aligns with the newer IEEE-754 direction: 754**-2019** `minimum`/`maximum` propagate `NaN` (whereas the older 754**-2008** `minNum`/`maxNum` — which is what CUDA's `fmaxf`/`fminf` follow — suppress it). So "propagate" is not a single universal rule for min/max, but it is what both dominant array libraries do and what the current IEEE revision moved to; the concrete ask is that `T.clamp` match `torch`/`numpy`. Whether that is achieved by making `T.clamp` `NaN`-transparent or by exposing an opt-in is the maintainers' call.

### Additional context

**Root cause.** `T.clamp` composes clamping out of `T.max`/`T.min`, whose CUDA lowering does not preserve `NaN`. `clamp` is defined as `T.min(T.max(dst, min_val), max_val)` at [`customize.py#L55-L56`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/tilelang/language/customize.py#L55); on CUDA `T.max`/`T.min` on floats emit `max`/`min`, i.e. `fmaxf`/`fminf`, which return the non-`NaN` argument. So `T.clamp(NaN, lo, hi)` computes `min(max(NaN, lo), hi) = min(lo, hi) = lo`.

<details>
<summary>Emitted CUDA + the T.max/T.min neighbor (both run on 0.1.13, L40S)</summary>

Emitted device expression for the repro:

```c++
C[((int)threadIdx.x)] = min(max(A[((int)threadIdx.x)], -0x1p+0f), 0x1p+0f);   // min(max(A[i], -1.0f), 1.0f)
```

The building blocks drop `NaN` on their own, so this is not specific to `clamp`:

```
T.max(nan, 0.0) -> 0.0    (torch.maximum -> nan)
T.min(nan, 0.0) -> 0.0    (torch.minimum -> nan)
```

A fix targeting `clamp`'s composition (e.g. an explicit `dst != dst` re-injection of `NaN`, or a `NaN`-propagating min/max) closes `T.clamp`; the `T.max`/`T.min` primitives keep the CUDA `fmaxf`/`fminf` behavior unless they are separately changed.
</details>

**Suggested fix.** One direction is to make `clamp` `NaN`-transparent — carry the input `NaN` through, or build it from a `NaN`-propagating min/max — so `T.clamp(NaN, …)` returns `NaN` like `torch.clamp`. Whether `T.max`/`T.min` themselves should also propagate `NaN` (vs keep the `fmaxf`/`fminf` reduction semantics used by softmax-style `m_i = T.max(m_i, …)` accumulators) is a separate call for the maintainers. Not built/verified.

**Provenance.** `clamp` was introduced in [#192](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/pull/192) ("[Language] Support clamp in language", merged 2025-03-12) with the `min(max(...))` body it still has; the `NaN`-dropping behavior has been present since then. Not a regression.

**Dedup.** I searched the open and closed tracker for `clamp` / `NaN` / `min max`. Distinct from [#2882](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/issues/2882) (`T.max`/`T.min` on two compile-time float **constants** fold order-dependently on `NaN` via the host `const_fold.h` path); that report treats the **runtime** `max(...)` lowering as the well-defined reference — this issue is that the runtime lowering itself drops `NaN` versus `torch.clamp`/`numpy.clip` (and IEEE-754-2019). No existing report covers `T.clamp`.

**Reach.** `T.clamp` is documented and appears in shipped examples. On 0.1.13 the cited sites are present and verbatim: `T.clamp(y_local[i,j] / y_s_local[i], fp8_min, fp8_max)` at `examples/cast/example_per_token_cast_to_fp8.py:35` and `example_group_per_split_token_cast_to_fp8.py:48`, and `T.clamp(x_local[i,j] / s_local[i], fp8_min/fp8_max)` at `examples/deepseek_v32/inference/kernel.py:72` and `examples/deepseek_v4/act_quant.py:78,156`. The underlying `T.max`/`T.min` appear in ~100 example sites (softmax `m_i = T.max(...)`, `T.max(x, 0)` ReLU).

I **ran** `example_per_token_cast_to_fp8.py`'s shipped kernel verbatim on 0.1.13 (L40S). Two results: (1) with the example's shipped input (`torch.randn`, all finite) the correctness check passes exactly — the shipped example **dodges** this bug because no `NaN` ever reaches the clamp, and no test in the tree injects one. (2) Injecting a single `NaN` into one input row of the same kernel makes that row diverge from the torch reference: torch propagates `NaN` across the whole 128-element group (row0 fp8 = `[nan, nan, …]`) while TileLang emits finite fp8 values (`[-448.0, -60.0, -384.0, …]`). So the bug is reachable through the shipped kernel; the shipped test just never exercises `NaN`. (This particular divergence is compounded by `T.reduce_absmax` also dropping the `NaN` by default — see the generalization table.) The trigger requires a `NaN` reaching the clamp; finite inputs clamp correctly (control passes). CI is green because no test asserts `NaN` propagation through `T.clamp`.

**Generalization.** Root, two levels: (a) SOURCE-level — `clamp` at `tilelang/language/customize.py#L55-L56` composes out of `T.max`/`T.min` (`tilelang/language/tir/ir.py:184-193` → TIR `min`/`max`), which lower to the CUDA NaN-dropping intrinsics (`fmaxf`/`fminf` for fp32, `__hmax`/`__hmin` for fp16/bf16 — never the `_nan` variants). (b) OPERATOR-level — every op built on scalar `T.max`/`T.min` inherits the drop: `T.clamp`, elementwise `T.max`/`T.min` themselves, and (by default) the `reduce_max`/`reduce_min`/`reduce_absmax` family. 4-axis sweep, all cells RUN on 0.1.13 (L40S):

| axis | cell tested (input → observed) | same-root? |
|---|---|---|
| related-operator | `T.max(nan,0.0)→0.0`, `T.min(nan,0.0)→0.0` (torch: `nan`); but `T.max(nan,nan)→nan` (`fmaxf` returns the other operand, so `NaN` survives only when BOTH are `NaN`) | same root (elementwise; the clamp building blocks) |
| related-operator | `T.reduce_absmax` fp32, default: `[…,nan,…]→3.0` (torch amax(abs)=`nan`) | same root, **distinct face** — reduce family has a `nan_propagate=True` opt-in (`reduce_op.py`, GH-#2697) that clamp lacks; but it **defaults to dropping** and is fp16/bf16-only |
| related-type | `T.clamp` fp16: `clamp(nan,-1,1)→-1.0` (device emits `__hmax`/`__hmin`, not `__hmax_nan`) | same root |
| related-type | `T.clamp` bf16: `clamp(nan,-1,1)→-1.0` (device emits `cutlass::bfloat16 __hmax/__hmin`) | same root |
| related-type | `T.clamp` int32/int (no `NaN` representation) | N/A — does not apply (integers have no `NaN`) |
| similar-logic | reduce family got a per-call `nan_propagate` escape hatch; elementwise `T.max`/`T.min`/`T.clamp` have NO such kwarg (`git grep nan_propagate` hits only `reduce_op.py`) | same root, asymmetric coverage — the fix already exists for reductions but not for the elementwise/clamp composition |

Framing kept **specific to `T.clamp`** (title/Problem unchanged): the elementwise `T.max`/`T.min` NaN-drop is arguably intended (softmax `m_i = T.max(...)` accumulators rely on `fmaxf` reduction semantics), and the reduce family already has an opt-in, so the crisp defect is that `T.clamp` — which per `torch.clamp`/IEEE should be `NaN`-transparent — has no way to preserve `NaN`. The reduce-default NaN-drop (`reduce_absmax` etc.) is a **distinct, adjacent** behavior with an existing opt-in and test coverage; not filed here.

**Impact.** Silent-wrong, deterministic, bounded to the clamped value: a `NaN` at the input becomes the `min` bound (`lo`) with no error, so a `NaN` that a workload relies on to detect (or propagate through a quantization step) is silently replaced by a finite in-range value every run. Fixing it aligns `T.clamp` with the `torch.clamp`/`numpy.clip` `NaN` semantics kernels are validated against (and the IEEE-754-2019 direction) and removes a silent frontend/runtime disagreement.

title: [BUG][wrong-code] A shared `T.gemm` operand sliced along MN silently reads the wrong K panel when `block_K` spans more than one swizzle atom
body:
## Summary

Passing a shared buffer **sliced along MN** as a `T.gemm` operand silently computes the wrong result whenever `block_K` spans more than one swizzle atom. No warning, no assertion, no illegal access — the kernel reads real data from the wrong place, so it just returns wrong numbers.

The same GEMM written with one shared buffer per slice is correct, which makes the slice/no-slice pair a clean A/B.

## Reproduction

`main@6af825e0`, H200 (sm_90a), CUDA 13.2, torch 2.13.

```python
import torch

import tilelang
import tilelang.language as T

M, N, K = 64, 128, 128
BM, BN, BK, W0 = 64, 128, 128, 64  # split BN into W0 + (BN - W0) = 64 + 64


def build(sliced: bool):
    @T.prim_func
    def main(
        a: T.Tensor((M, K), "bfloat16"),
        b: T.Tensor((N, K), "bfloat16"),
        c: T.Tensor((M, N), "bfloat16"),
    ):
        with T.Kernel(T.ceildiv(N, BN), T.ceildiv(M, BM), threads=128) as (bx, by):
            a_s = T.alloc_shared((BM, BK), "bfloat16")
            c0 = T.alloc_fragment((BM, W0), "float32")
            c1 = T.alloc_fragment((BM, BN - W0), "float32")
            T.clear(c0)
            T.clear(c1)
            if sliced:
                # One shared buffer, consumed as two row slices.
                b_s = T.alloc_shared((BN, BK), "bfloat16")
            else:
                # Same math, one buffer per slice.
                b_s0 = T.alloc_shared((W0, BK), "bfloat16")
                b_s1 = T.alloc_shared((BN - W0, BK), "bfloat16")
            for ko in T.Pipelined(T.ceildiv(K, BK), num_stages=0):
                T.copy(a[by * BM, ko * BK], a_s)
                if sliced:
                    T.copy(b[bx * BN, ko * BK], b_s)
                    T.gemm(a_s, b_s[0:W0, :], c0, transpose_B=True)
                    T.gemm(a_s, b_s[W0:BN, :], c1, transpose_B=True)
                else:
                    T.copy(b[bx * BN, ko * BK], b_s0)
                    T.copy(b[bx * BN + W0, ko * BK], b_s1)
                    T.gemm(a_s, b_s0, c0, transpose_B=True)
                    T.gemm(a_s, b_s1, c1, transpose_B=True)
            T.copy(c0, c[by * BM, bx * BN])
            T.copy(c1, c[by * BM, bx * BN + W0])

    return tilelang.compile(main, out_idx=[2], target="cuda")


torch.manual_seed(0)
a = torch.randn(M, K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
b = torch.randn(N, K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ref = a.float() @ b.float().T

for sliced in (False, True):
    err = (build(sliced)(a, b).float() - ref).abs().max().item()
    print(f"{'one buffer, two slices' if sliced else 'two buffers      ':22s}  max_err = {err:.4f}")
```

```
two buffers             max_err = 0.1248     <- bf16 accumulation noise
one buffer, two slices  max_err = 43.3982    <- wrong
```

## Scope

Both operands and both slice axes, `block_M = block_N = 128`, slicing 64 + 64:

| operand | `block_K=64` | `block_K=128` | `block_K=256` |
|---|---|---|---|
| K-major A (`A_s[0:64, :]`) | ok | **err ≈ 113** | **err ≈ 121** |
| K-major B (`B_s[0:64, :]`, `transpose_B=True`) | ok | **err ≈ 101** | **err ≈ 107** |
| MN-major A (`A_s[:, 0:64]`, `transpose_A=True`) | ok | ok | ok |
| MN-major B (`B_s[:, 0:64]`) | ok | ok | ok |

Independent of `threads`, `num_stages`, warp specialization, and dtype (fp16 and bf16 both). MN-major operands are unaffected — that branch of the offset formula does not use the term below.

`block_K = 64` is correct only by accident: at bf16 that is exactly one 128B swizzle atom, so the buggy term is multiplied by zero (see below).

## Root cause

`tilelang/cuda/intrinsics/macro/wgmma_macro_generator.py`, `wgmma_ss_atom` / `wgmma_rs_atom`:

```python
B_offset = (ki // bk_atom_size) * n_dim * b_swizzle_atom_elems + ...
```

When `block_K` exceeds one swizzle atom, the shared layout splits the K axis into panels and stores them **panel-major**. A `(128, 128)` bf16 tile decodes as

```
Sw<3,3,3> o 0 o (128,(64,2)):(64,(1,8192))
                              ^^^^ panel stride = 128 rows x 64 elems
```

so advancing to the next K panel steps by **the buffer's** MN extent. The formula instead reconstructs that step from `n_dim`, the extent of *this operand*. The two coincide only when the operand covers the whole buffer; for a slice `n_dim` shrinks while the panel spacing does not.

Concretely, for the repro above (bf16, 64-element atom, `bk_atom_size = 4`, so `ki // 4` selects the panel):

| operand | slice origin (correct) | `ki >= 4` should read | actually reads |
|---|---|---|---|
| `b_s[0:64, :]` | elem 0 | 8192 = row 0, panel 1 | 4096 = **row 64, panel 0** |
| `b_s[64:128, :]` | 4096 ✓ | 12288 = row 64, panel 1 | 8192 = **row 0, panel 1** |

Emitted CUDA — the panel step is 8192 bytes where it should be 16384:

```cpp
tl::initialize_wgmma_descriptor<1, 1, 64>(desc_b_1, (char*)&b_s[0] + 8192);  // origin: correct
tl::wgmma_ss<...>(..., desc_b_1 + (((ki >> 2) * 8192 + (ki & 3) * 32) >> 4), ...);
//                                            ^^^^ should be 16384
```

Two consequences worth calling out:

- The **slice origin is correct** (`slice_byte_offset` is derived from the layout). Only the panel step is wrong, so the first K atom of every operand is right and everything past it is wrong — the error is a partial-garbage mix rather than an obvious blow-up.
- The two slices read **each other's rows**, all within the buffer, so there is no out-of-bounds signal.

The same expression is duplicated in five more places, all with the same defect:

- `wgmma_sp_macro_generator.py` — sparse Hopper, `wgmma_ss` and `wgmma_rs`
- `tcgen05_macro_generator.py` — Blackwell, `tcgen05_ss_atom`, `tcgen05_ts_atom`, `tcgen05_blockscaled_atom`

## Why nothing caught it

`tilelang/language/gemm_op.py` used to assert `A_offset[-2] == 0`, i.e. reject an operand with a non-zero offset on the second-to-last axis. That assertion was dropped when the region-based lowering landed, on the premise that "every lowering consumes the complete operand BufferRegions". That is half true: the *origin* is consumed from the region correctly, but the *panel stride* is still reconstructed from emitter-level tile dims. The guard was removed and no equivalent check replaced it.

Existing coverage misses it on both backends:

- `test_tilelang_kernel_gemm_with_stride.py` does slice a shared operand, but at `block_K = 32` (single atom) and on the pre-Hopper `mma` path.
- `test_tilelang_language_tcgen05_sliced_operands.py` slices only along **K**, which is exactly the axis where the panel term is unused. MN slicing is validated for atom alignment but never numerically.

## Environment

- tilelang `main@6af825e0`
- H200 (sm_90a), nvcc 13.2, driver 595.71.05, torch 2.13.0+cu130
- Also reproduces with `TL_DISABLE_WARP_SPECIALIZED` both on and off

I have a fix and will open a PR shortly.

title: [BUG][Fuzzer][ice-on-valid-code] `T.fill`/`T.clear` of an `int4` buffer crashes the compiler with `broadcast_var is not a constant` instead of emitting the fill
body:
### Required prerequisites - [x] I have read the documentation . - [x] I have searched the [Issue Tracker](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/issues) that this hasn't already been reported. (comment there if it has.) ### What version of TileLang are you using? 0.1.13 (latest release) ### System information - TileLang 0.1.13, Python 3.13, Linux. - GPU: NVIDIA L40S (compute capability 8.9, sm_89). The defect is in the CUDA `Broadcast` codegen (`src/cuda/codegen/codegen_cuda.cc`), which runs at code-generation time before any arch-specific lowering, so it is architecture-independent. ### Problem description `T.fill` (and `T.clear`, which lowers to `T.fill(..., 0)`) on an `int4` buffer aborts at compile time with ``` InternalError: Check failed: (p) is false: BroadcastNode ... value: broadcast_var is not a constant ``` `int4` is a supported element dtype (it is the operand dtype of the shipped `examples/gemm_int4` kernel) and `T.fill`/`T.clear` place no dtype restriction on the buffer, so the kernel is legal. The fill lowering broadcasts the fill value across the vectorized store, but binds that value to a temporary (`broadcast_var`) first, so the `Broadcast` node's value is a `Var`, not a constant. The `int4` branch of the CUDA `Broadcast` visitor unconditionally requires a constant value (`ICHECK(p)` on `as_const_int(op->value)`), so it fatal-aborts. The identical kernel on the sibling `int8` dtype compiles, because the `int8` branch only special-cases the constant sub-case and otherwise falls through to the generic (non-constant) path. The crash does not depend on `T.copy` or on any GEMM machinery — a bare `T.fill`/`T.clear` of an `int4` shared buffer reproduces it. Not a regression — see Provenance. ### Reproducible example code ```python import tilelang, tilelang.language as T M, N = 16, 64 def make(dtype): @T.prim_func def func(B: T.Tensor((M, N), dtype)): with T.Kernel(1, threads=128): sh = T.alloc_shared((M, N), dtype) T.fill(sh, 1) # T.clear(sh) fails identically T.copy(sh, B) return func def try_compile(dtype): try: tilelang.compile(make(dtype)).get_kernel_source() return "compiled" except Exception as e: return "CRASH: " + str(e).splitlines()[-1] print("int4:", try_compile("int4")) # -> CRASH ("broadcast_var is not a constant") print("int8:", try_compile("int8")) # -> compiled (control) ``` Output: ``` int4: CRASH: Check failed: (p) is false: BroadcastNode 0x... value: broadcast_var is not a constant int8: compiled ``` ### Traceback ``` tvm.error.InternalError: Check failed: (p) is false: BroadcastNode 0x... value: broadcast_var is not a constant ... CodeGenTileLangCUDA::VisitStmt_(BufferStoreNode const*) CodeGenC::PrintExpr(PrimExpr const&) CodeGenTileLangCUDA::VisitExpr_(BroadcastNode const*, std::ostream&) tvm::runtime::detail::LogFatalImpl(...) ``` ### Expected behavior Filling an `int4` buffer with a runtime (non-constant) broadcast value should emit code rather than aborting, matching what the sibling `int8` path already does: the `int8` branch handles the constant case as an optimization and otherwise falls through to the generic `Broadcast` lowering, so a variable fill value is fine there. The `int4` branch could take the same shape — keep the constant fast-path, and fall through for a non-constant value instead of asserting. ### Additional context **Root cause.** The CUDA `Broadcast` codegen does not handle a non-constant value in its `int4` branch. In [`CodeGenTileLangCUDA::VisitExpr_(BroadcastNode)`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/src/cuda/codegen/codegen_cuda.cc#L5614-L5618) the `int4` (`bits() == 4`) branch reads `p = as_const_int(op->value)` and immediately `ICHECK(p) << "... is not a constant"`, so any broadcast of a `Var` fatal-aborts. The `broadcast_var` in the message is *not* something `T.fill` wrote — it is created by the device-lowering pass [`HoistBroadcastValues`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/tilelang/transform/hoist_broadcast_values.py), which runs unconditionally in `engine/lower.py` (`device_mod = tilelang.transform.HoistBroadcastValues()(device_mod)`). That pass deliberately takes a `Broadcast` of an *immediate constant* (`IntImm`/`FloatImm`) and rebinds the constant to a let-bound `Var` named `broadcast_var`, leaving a `Broadcast(broadcast_var, lanes)` behind. So a fill value that was a constant in the frontend is a `Var` by the time codegen runs, and `as_const_int` returns null. Verified this session: the same crash fires on a *genuinely* runtime fill value (a kernel scalar argument, no hoist pass involved) with the message `value: T.Cast("int4", s) is not a constant` — the `int4` branch cannot emit any non-constant broadcast, hoisted or not.
Why the int8 control compiles The [`int8` branch of the same visitor](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/src/cuda/codegen/codegen_cuda.cc#L5503-L5525) guards its constant packing with `if (p) { ... }` and returns only inside it; when `p` is null it does not `return`, so control reaches the generic `Broadcast` path lower in the function. The `int4` branch instead asserts on `p` before doing anything, so it has no non-constant fall-through.
**Suggested fix.** Give the `int4` branch the same structure as the `int8` one: gate the constant packing on `if (p)` and, when the value is not a constant, fall through to the generic `Broadcast` lowering rather than `ICHECK`-aborting. **Provenance.** The `int4` `Broadcast` branch (with the unconditional `ICHECK(p)`) was introduced in [#2073](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/pull/2073) ("[CUDA] Improve int4 GEMM lowering and packed codegen support", 2026-04-22); a later namespace refactor ([#2297](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/pull/2297)) relocated but did not change it. When it was written, a constant fill value still reached codegen as an `IntImm`, so the `ICHECK(p)` held for the fill/clear path. The `HoistBroadcastValues` pass that rebinds those constants to a `Var` was added three weeks later in [#2166](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/pull/2166) (first commit 2026-05-12) and wired into the default device-lowering pipeline — this is what turns the fill value non-constant before it reaches the branch. So the fill/clear crash is best described as a **regression by pass interaction**: neither PR is wrong alone, but the hoist pass now feeds the `int4` branch exactly the non-constant input its `ICHECK` forbids. (The branch was independently already broken for a *truly* runtime broadcast value, which no shipped kernel produces.) **Dedup.** I searched the open and closed tracker and found no existing report of this defect. **Generalization (root + 4-axis sweep, all cells RUN this session on sm_89 / v0.1.13).** Two-level root: - **Source-level root:** `CodeGenTileLangCUDA::VisitExpr_(BroadcastNode)`, the `(is_int()||is_uint()) && bits()==4` branch (codegen_cuda.cc:5614–5618). Fragile idiom = *assert-constant before doing anything*, with no non-constant fall-through — versus every other width's *gate on `if(p)` then fall through*. It is the only `as_const_int(op->value)`-gated branch in the whole visitor that `ICHECK`s instead of guarding (the int8 site at 5504 is the safe twin). - **Operator-level root:** any store into an `int4` buffer whose stored value lowers to a *vectorized `Broadcast`*. `T.fill`/`T.clear` are the frontend triggers, but so is a raw vectorized assignment of a scalar. Two independent ways to make the value non-constant both hit it: the `HoistBroadcastValues` pass (constant → `Var`) and a genuinely runtime scalar. | axis | cell tested | result | same-root? | |---|---|---|---| | related-type | `uint4` fill | CRASH `broadcast_var is not a constant` | **same** (shares the 4-bit branch; not signedness-gated) | | related-type | `int1` fill | CRASH `Cannot convert type int1x4 to CUDA type!` | **distinct** — falls through to the generic `make_` path, dies in `PrintType` (int1 codegen gap at :2321), not the `ICHECK` | | related-type | `float4_e2m1fn` (fp4) fill | compiled | distinct path — fp4 is excluded by `!is_float4()`, routed through the fp8/fp4 branch (:5776); confirms the predicate boundary | | related-type | `int8` / `int16` / `int32` fill | compiled | control — 8-bit gates on `if(p)`, wider ints take generic path | | related-type | `float16` / `bfloat16` / `float8_e4m3` / `float8_e5m2` / `float32` fill | compiled | control — those branches `PrintExpr` the (Var) value | | related-operator | `T.clear(int4)` | CRASH (same msg) | **same** — `clear` = `fill(...,0)` | | related-operator | `T.fill(int4, 0)` / `(int4, 7)` | CRASH (same msg) | **same** — value magnitude irrelevant | | related-operator | raw vectorized store of a runtime scalar into int4 | CRASH `value: T.Cast("int4", s) is not a constant` | **same** — direct non-constant, no hoist pass; proves the branch is broken for real runtime values too | | similar-logic | int8 branch fed a genuinely runtime scalar (the safe twin) | compiled | control — same idiom done with `if(p)` fall-through | | related-source | other `as_const_int(op->value)` sites in the visitor | only two exist (int8 :5504 safe, int4 :5616 buggy) | single buggy instance — no other sibling to fix | **Boundary is narrow and stays specific.** The defect is exactly the one 4-bit integer branch; `int4` and `uint4` are the *same* branch (one fix covers both), so this is not a per-dtype family but a single missing fall-through. Adjacent widths, fp4, and the int8 twin are all clean. Title/Problem kept specific to the 4-bit `Broadcast` branch. **Distinct-adjacent bug found (not filed).** `T.fill` of an `int1` buffer also aborts, but with a *different* root: `Cannot convert type int1x4 to CUDA type!` in `PrintType` (the int1 codegen at codegen_cuda.cc:2321 area), reached via the generic `make_` fall-through — not the `ICHECK(p)`. Different mechanism, different fix; recorded here, not filed. **Impact.** The trigger is narrow: it needs a broadcast store into an `int4` buffer, and no shipped kernel does this (the one int4-buffer example, `gemm_int4`, only clears its `int32` accumulator — verified by running it). Any `T.fill`/`T.clear` of an `int4` buffer fires it, because `HoistBroadcastValues` makes even a constant fill value non-constant before codegen; a genuinely runtime broadcast store fires it too. When it fires it is a compile-time `ICHECK` abort — loud and caught immediately when building that kernel; nothing is silently miscompiled and no wrong value can reach a run. Fixing it closes a dtype-parity gap so a legal `T.fill`/`T.clear` on `int4` compiles the way it already does on `int8`, rather than refusing to build. **Reach.** (Example run this session, v0.1.13 / sm_89.) The only shipped example that allocates real `T.int4` buffers is `examples/gemm_int4/example_tilelang_gemm_int4.py` — `A_shared`/`B_shared` are `T.alloc_shared(..., T.int4)`. I ran that example verbatim (its default `check_int4_gemm_correctness()` config): it **compiles and prints `Correctness check passed.`** It dodges this bug because it only `T.clear`s the `int32` accumulator `C_local` (line 29) and loads the `int4` operands via `T.copy`, never filling the `int4` buffers themselves — so no shipped kernel fills an `int4` buffer, which is why CI is green. Adding a single `T.clear(A_shared)` to that example-shaped kernel reproduces the crash (ran this session → `broadcast_var is not a constant`). Correction to an earlier claim in this draft: the `examples/dequantize_gemm/` kernels do **not** use `int4` buffers — they carry the 4-bit weights in a packed `storage_dtype` (int8/int32) and dequantize into an `in_dtype` (fp16/bf16) buffer, so none of them allocate or fill a `T.int4` buffer or exercise this branch. `gemm_int4` is the sole shipped int4-buffer site.

title: [Perf] Lower T.any_of / T.all_of via warp vote intrinsics (__any_sync / __all_sync) where safe
body:
## Current behavior

`T.any_of(buffer)` / `T.all_of(buffer)` (`tilelang/language/logical.py`) lower through the `tl.any_of` / `tl.all_of` builtins (`src/op/logical.cc`) to `call_extern` of the device helpers `tl::Any` / `tl::All` (`src/tl_templates/cuda/common.h:846-863`, HIP equivalents at `src/tl_templates/hip/common.h:304-322`):

```cpp
template <typename T> TL_DEVICE bool Any(T *a, int size) {
  for (int i = 0; i < size; i++)
    if (a[i]) return true;
  return false;
}
```

Every thread scans the buffer serially and independently. Two costs:

- **Shared buffers:** all 32 lanes of a warp redundantly read all `size` elements — 32x redundant shared-memory traffic per warp, and the loop is O(size) per thread.
- **Fragments:** each thread reduces only its own local slice, so callers that want a tile-wide / warp-uniform answer still need a manual cross-thread combine (typically a shared-memory round-trip).

## Proposal

Use the warp vote intrinsics that #1858 already wired end-to-end (`tl.any_sync` / `tl.all_sync` → `__any_sync` / `__all_sync` on CUDA at `src/cuda/codegen/codegen_cuda.cc:4492`, `__any` / `__all` on HIP at `src/rocm/codegen/codegen_hip.cc:1589`):

**1. Shared/global buffers — cooperative warp-strided scan + one vote:**

```cpp
template <typename T> TL_DEVICE bool AnyWarp(T *a, int size, uint32_t mask = 0xffffffff) {
  bool local = false;
  for (int i = (threadIdx.x % 32); i < size; i += 32)
    local |= static_cast<bool>(a[i]);
  return __any_sync(mask, local);   // AllWarp: &= + __all_sync
}
```

Per-thread reads drop by the warp size (32x on CUDA, 64x on CDNA wavefronts), and the result is warp-uniform.

**2. Fragments — fold the warp with one vote:** keep the per-thread local scan, then `__any_sync` combines the 32 partials in a single instruction, replacing the shared-memory staging a tile-wide reduction needs today.

## Why this cannot be a blanket replacement

- **Convergence:** `__*_sync` requires every lane in the mask to reach the instruction. The current `tl::Any` is purely thread-local and is legal in divergent control flow (e.g. under `if (tid == 0)`); a vote at such a call site is UB on Volta+. The lowering must either prove the call site warp-uniform or keep the cooperative path opt-in.
- **Fragment semantics change** from "per-thread partial over the local slice" to "warp-uniform" — this must be a new variant, not an in-place swap.
- **Short-circuiting:** `all_of` currently early-exits on the first false; each lane can still break within its own stride, and a chunked ballot-based early exit can recover most of the rest.

## Suggested implementation plan

1. Add `tl::AnyWarp` / `tl::AllWarp` device templates to `src/tl_templates/cuda/common.h` and the HIP equivalents (`__any`/`__all`, wavefront-width stride) to `src/tl_templates/hip/common.h`.
2. First step (conservative): an explicit opt-in, e.g. `T.any_of(buf, scope="warp")`, that selects the cooperative lowering in the `FLowerIntrinsic` hooks in `src/op/logical.cc`, leaving convergence responsibility with the caller.
3. Follow-up: dispatch automatically when the buffer scope is shared and the call site is provably warp-uniform (outside thread-divergent control flow in the tile-op body).
4. Tests alongside the existing `testing/python/language/test_tilelang_language_any_of.py` / `test_tilelang_language_all_of.py`: numerical equivalence vs. the serial path for shared and fragment buffers on CUDA and HIP, plus a documented-constraint test for divergent call sites.

title: [BUG][Fuzzer][ice-on-valid-code] `T.loop_break()` inside `T.unroll(explicit=True)` emits bare `break;` outside any loop, so nvcc rejects the kernel instead of it compiling
body:
### Required prerequisites - [x] I have read the documentation . - [x] I have searched the [Issue Tracker](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/issues) that this hasn't already been reported. (comment there if it has.) ### What version of TileLang are you using? 0.1.13 ### System information TileLang 0.1.13; CUDA 13.0 (nvcc), PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; NVIDIA L40S (sm_89). ### Problem description A `T.loop_break()` inside a `for i in T.unroll(N, explicit=True)` loop makes the kernel fail to compile: nvcc reports `N` copies of `error: a break statement may only be used within a loop or switch`. `explicit=True` fully expands the loop body into `N` inline copies with **no surrounding loop**. The body contains a `T.loop_break()`, which codegen lowers verbatim to `break;`, so each of the `N` unrolled copies emits a bare `break;` at kernel scope. Both `T.unroll(..., explicit=True)` and `T.loop_break()` are documented, supported primitives, so this is legal input that fails to compile. The same kernel with `explicit=False` (the default) keeps the surrounding `for` loop and compiles, giving a working control in the repro below. Not a regression in the sense of "used to work": the explicit-unroll full-expansion path has behaved this way since it was added (see Provenance).
Emitted CUDA (N=8): 8 body copies, each with a bare break;, no enclosing loop ```cuda extern "C" __global__ void bug_kernel(const int* __restrict__ A, int* __restrict__ C) { C[0] = A[0]; if (5 < A[0]) { break; } C[1] = A[1]; if (5 < A[1]) { break; } // ... 6 more identical copies ... C[7] = A[7]; if (5 < A[7]) { break; } } ``` nvcc: `8 errors detected` — one `a break statement may only be used within a loop or switch` per copy.
### Reproducible example code ```python import tilelang, tilelang.language as T N = 8 # BUG: explicit=True fully expands the body into N inline copies with NO surrounding # loop; the T.loop_break() in each copy becomes a bare `break;` -> nvcc rejects it. @T.prim_func def bug(A: T.Tensor((N,), "int32"), C: T.Tensor((N,), "int32")): with T.Kernel(1, threads=1): for i in T.unroll(N, explicit=True): C[i] = A[i] if A[i] > 5: T.loop_break() # CONTROL: explicit=False keeps the surrounding for-loop, so the break is inside a # loop and the kernel compiles. @T.prim_func def ok(A: T.Tensor((N,), "int32"), C: T.Tensor((N,), "int32")): with T.Kernel(1, threads=1): for i in T.unroll(N, explicit=False): C[i] = A[i] if A[i] > 5: T.loop_break() tilelang.compile(ok, out_idx=[1]) # -> compiles tilelang.compile(bug, out_idx=[1]) # -> RuntimeError: 8 errors, "a break statement may only be used within a loop or switch" ``` ### Traceback
nvcc error (truncated to the first two of 8 copies) ``` tvm_kernels.cu(21): error: a break statement may only be used within a loop or switch break; tvm_kernels.cu(25): error: a break statement may only be used within a loop or switch break; ... 8 errors detected in the compilation of "tvm_kernels.cu". ```
### Expected behavior The kernel should compile. `T.loop_break()` is documented ("Break from current loop") and `T.unroll(explicit=True)` is a documented, typed option, so their combination should either preserve the exit semantics or be rejected cleanly at compile time rather than emitting a `break;` that nvcc rejects. The `explicit=False` path already handles the same source correctly by keeping the loop. ### Additional context **Root cause.** The `UnrollLoop` pass does not account for a `loop_break` in the body when it fully expands an explicit-unrolled loop, so it emits a `break` with no enclosing loop. Concretely, [`LoopUnroller::Unroll`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/src/transform/unroll_loop.cc#L280-L298) substitutes the loop variable and returns `SeqStmt::Flatten(unrolled)` — a flat sequence of `N` body copies with the `For` node discarded. This path is taken for explicit unroll ([unroll_loop.cc#L211-L214](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/src/transform/unroll_loop.cc#L211-L214)). CUDA codegen then lowers the `tl.loop_break` intrinsic unconditionally to `break;` ([codegen_cuda.cc#L2912-L2914](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/src/cuda/codegen/codegen_cuda.cc#L2912-L2914)), so each copy carries a bare `break;`. **Suggested fix.** One direction: detect a `loop_break` (or any early-exit intrinsic) in the body and decline explicit full-expansion for that loop — fall back to the pragma-unroll form that keeps the `For`, as `explicit=False` already does. Alternatively, reject the combination at frontend/lowering time with a clear message. Which is appropriate depends on whether explicit unroll is meant to support early exit at all — a call for the maintainers. **Provenance.** The `SeqStmt::Flatten` full-expansion in the explicit-unroll path has been present at least since [#1654](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/pull/1654) (merged 2026-01-12); the `tl.loop_break` → `break;` codegen since [#563](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/pull/563) (merged 2025-06-11). The interaction has been broken no later than #1654; origin before that is unverified. No review bot flagged it. **Dedup.** Searched the open and closed tracker (`loop_break`, `unroll break`, `explicit unroll`). Distinct from [#2608](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/issues/2608) (`break`/`T.loop_break()` inside `T.vectorized`): that concerns a different pass (VectorizeLoop). On 0.1.13 the vectorized case does not hit this defect at all — a `loop_break` in the body blocks vectorization, so the loop falls back to serial and the `break;` stays inside a real `for` loop and compiles (verified locally, see Reach). This report is the `UnrollLoop` explicit-expansion path, which discards the `For` entirely and produces a hard nvcc compile error. No other report of this defect. **Reach.** `T.loop_break()` is documented at [`docs/programming_guides/instructions.md`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/docs/programming_guides/instructions.md?plain=1#L231) but demonstrated in no `examples/`/`testing/` file (`grep`: 0 sites outside the language definitions). `T.unroll(explicit=True)` is a documented, typed keyword (`explicit: bool = False` at [`loop.py#L240`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/tilelang/language/loop.py?plain=1#L240)); `T.unroll` appears in 7 example files but none pass `explicit=True` (`grep`: 0 `explicit=True` sites in `examples/` or `testing/`). The bug is the intersection of these two documented-but-rarely-combined ingredients; it fires on any constant trip count `N` (each of the `N` copies emits a `break;`). No test exercises `loop_break` under explicit unroll, which is why CI is green. The same `T.loop_break()` in the three adjacent loop forms all compiled on 0.1.13, isolating the defect to the explicit-unroll expansion (verified this session): | loop form (same body) | result | |---|---| | `T.unroll(N, explicit=True)` | **fails** — `N` bare `break;`, nvcc rejects (this bug) | | `T.unroll(N, explicit=False)` (default) | compiles — keeps the `for`, `break;` is inside it | | `T.serial(N)` | compiles — real loop, `break;` inside it | | `T.vectorized(N)` | compiles — `loop_break` blocks the vectorization plan, falls back to a serial `for` (a warning is emitted), `break;` stays inside it | Only the explicit-unroll path drops the enclosing `For` (via `SeqStmt::Flatten`), which is what strands the `break;`. **Generalization (verified this session, 0.1.13, sm_89).** *Two-level root.* (a) SOURCE-level: `LoopUnroller::Unroll` in `src/transform/unroll_loop.cc` (L280-298) full-expands the loop body with `SeqStmt::Flatten` and discards the `For`, with no check for a `loop_break` in the body; the sole raw loop-control emitter is CUDA codegen `tl::loop_break()` → `break;` (`codegen_cuda.cc` L2912-2914). (b) OPERATOR-level: any `For` that reaches the full-expansion `Unroll()` call site (explicit unroll, and the extent-1 auto branch at L211-213) combined with a `loop_break` that targets *that* loop. `loop_break` is the ONLY intrinsic that codegens to a bare loop-control statement — there is no `continue`/`return` sibling intrinsic (grep of codegen: `break;` is the only such emit), so the related-operator "sibling raw-stmt intrinsic" axis has no other cell to test. | axis | cell tested | result | same-root? | |---|---|---|---| | related-source | extent-1 explicit unroll (`N=1`) | **FAILED**, 1 stranded `break;` — the `auto_max_extent_==1` branch also calls `Unroll()` | yes | | related-type (knob) | non-unit `start=2, stop=16, step=3` | **FAILED**, 5 stranded `break;` (= ceil((16−2)/3)) | yes | | related-source | `break` belongs to the outer explicit-unroll loop, placed after an inner `T.serial` loop | **FAILED**, 4 stranded `break;` — the outer `For` is discarded; the surviving inner loop does not rescue it | yes | | similar-logic | inner `break` inside an inner `T.serial` under an outer explicit unroll (break targets the kept inner loop) | COMPILED, 4 `break;` each inside its own real `for` | boundary — break must target the *expanded* loop | | related-operator (loop form) | `unroll_factor=N` (explicit=False) | COMPILED, keeps the `for` (pragma unroll, not full-expansion) | distinct path | | related-operator (loop form) | `T.Pipelined(N, num_stages=1)` | COMPILED, keeps the `for` | distinct path | | related-operator (loop form) | `T.serial(N)` | COMPILED (real loop) | distinct path | | related-operator (loop form) | `T.vectorized(N)` | COMPILED — `loop_break` blocks the vectorization plan, falls back to a serial `for` | distinct path | Net: the defect is exactly the `Unroll()` full-expansion path (explicit unroll of any constant trip count, including the extent-1 auto branch), fired whenever a `loop_break` targets the loop being expanded. Non-unit start/step and extent-1 all reproduce (same root); every non-expanding loop form and a break that targets a *kept* inner loop are clean. The boundary is narrow but the class is "loop_break targeting a fully-expanded loop", not literally "explicit=True with default start". No adjacent distinct bug was found while sweeping; no new bug found. **Example-run (PART 1).** There is no shipped example to run verbatim: `T.loop_break` appears in NO `examples/` or `testing/` file on 0.1.13 (`git grep loop_break v0.1.13 -- examples testing` → 0 hits; it exists only in `docs/`, `src/`, and `tilelang/language/`), and no `examples/`/`testing/` file passes `explicit=True` (0 hits). So the Reach claim "demonstrated in no example file" is confirmed by direct grep, and there is no shipped file that either exercises or dodges the bug. In lieu of an example, the four loop-form controls in the table above were RUN (results as shown), plus the primary repro (8 stranded `break;`, nvcc `8 errors detected`). **Impact.** The trigger is narrow (a `loop_break` under `explicit=True` unroll). When it fires it is a hard compile error, not silent — nvcc rejects the kernel and it never runs, so it is caught immediately rather than corrupting results. Fixing it closes a documented-primitive combination that currently cannot compile, and removes the divergence from the `explicit=False` path that already handles the same source.

title: [BUG] export_library fails on disk-cache hit even with execution_backend="tvm_ffi"
body:
### Required prerequisites

- [x] I have read the documentation <https://tilelang.com>.
- [x] I have searched the [Issue Tracker](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/issues) that this hasn't already been reported. (comment there if it has.)

### What version of TileLang are you using?

0.1.13+cuda.gitddf3bdcb

### System information

- Installed from source (editable install, uv-managed)
- Python 3.11.13, torch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, Linux

### Problem description

`kernel.export_library(...)` works on a **cold compile** but always raises `AttributeError: Runtime module is not available` on the **second run** (when the compiled kernel is loaded from the on-disk cache), even though the kernel was compiled with `execution_backend="tvm_ffi"`.

Root cause: on a cache hit, `JITKernel.from_database` (`tilelang/jit/kernel.py:150-193`) rebuilds only the adapter and **never populates `self.artifact`**. `export_library` (`tilelang/jit/kernel.py:737-763`) checks `self.artifact is None or self.artifact.rt_mod is None` and raises. On a fresh compile, `_compile_artifact` → `lower_with_context(enable_host_codegen=True)` sets `artifact.rt_mod = host_mod` (`tilelang/engine/lower.py:193-204`), so export works.

Additional finding: even if `artifact.rt_mod` were set to the module loaded from the cache (`runtime.load_module(kernel_lib_path)`), TVM's `Module.export_library` cannot re-export it — `is_compilation_exportable()` is `False` and it raises `RuntimeError: Module[library] does not support SaveToBytes`. The cached `executable.so` **is** already the exported library, so a viable fix is to copy it, or otherwise record the exported library path on the kernel.


### Reproducible example code

```python
import torch
import tilelang
import tilelang.language as T

@tilelang.jit(execution_backend="tvm_ffi")
def gemm_relu_eager(A, B, block_M=64, block_N=64, block_K=32, num_stages=2,
                    dtype=T.float16, accum_dtype=T.float32):
    M, N, K = T.const("M, N, K")
    A: T.Tensor((M, K), dtype)
    B: T.Tensor((K, N), dtype)
    C = T.empty((M, N), dtype)
    with T.Kernel(T.ceildiv(N, block_N), T.ceildiv(M, block_M), threads=128) as (bx, by):
        A_shared = T.alloc_shared((block_M, block_K), dtype)
        B_shared = T.alloc_shared((block_K, block_N), dtype)
        C_local = T.alloc_fragment((block_M, block_N), accum_dtype)
        T.clear(C_local)
        for ko in T.Pipelined(T.ceildiv(K, block_K), num_stages=num_stages):
            T.copy(A[by * block_M, ko * block_K], A_shared)
            T.copy(B[ko * block_K, bx * block_N], B_shared)
            T.gemm(A_shared, B_shared, C_local)
        for i, j in T.Parallel(block_M, block_N):
            C_local[i, j] = T.max(C_local[i, j], 0)
        T.copy(C_local, C[by * block_M, bx * block_N])
    return C

kernel = gemm_relu_eager.compile(M=1024, N=1024, K=1024)
print("backend:", kernel.execution_backend)
kernel.export_library("gemm_relu.so")

# Run the script a second time (same process env, disk cache populated):
# the second run fails before reaching export_library.
```


### Traceback

```pytb
TileLang begins to compile kernel `gemm_relu_eager` with `out_idx=[-1]`   # only on first run
TileLang completes to compile kernel `gemm_relu_eager`                     # only on first run
backend: tvm_ffi
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 34, in <module>
    kernel.export_library("gemm_relu.so")
  File "/path/to/tilelang/tilelang/jit/kernel.py", line 754, in export_library
    raise AttributeError(
AttributeError: Runtime module is not available. Please compile the kernel with `execution_backend="tvm_ffi"` before exporting.
```

### Expected behavior

`export_library` should succeed regardless of whether the kernel came from a fresh compile or the disk cache (as long as the backend supports export, e.g. `tvm_ffi`).

**Additional context**

Suspect locations:
- `tilelang/jit/kernel.py:150-193` — `from_database` never sets `self.artifact`
- `tilelang/jit/kernel.py:753-762` — `export_library` assumes `artifact.rt_mod` is present
- `tilelang/jit/adapter/tvm_ffi.py:337-380` — `from_database` loads the executable via `runtime.load_module(kernel_lib_path)` but the loaded module cannot be re-exported by TVM


### Additional context

_No response_

title: [BUG][Fuzzer][ice-on-valid-code] Logical `T.Not` on a `bool` buffer in an auto-vectorized loop emits `!ushort4`, crashing nvcc instead of negating lane-by-lane
body:
### Required prerequisites - [x] I have read the documentation . - [x] I have searched the [Issue Tracker](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/issues) that this hasn't already been reported. (comment there if it has.) ### What version of TileLang are you using? 0.1.13 ### System information TileLang 0.1.13; L40S (sm_89), CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.8.0, Python 3.13. ### Problem description A logical NOT (`T.Not` or Python `not`) applied elementwise inside a `T.Parallel` loop fails to compile whenever the loop auto-vectorizes (more than one element per thread). The emitted CUDA applies the scalar operator `!` directly to a vector operand, and nvcc rejects it: (Note: `~` on a `bool` buffer routes through a *different* visitor and emits `~ushortN` — see "Class" below; that is the bitwise sibling, filed separately. This issue is specifically the `!` / `NotNode` site.) ``` tvm_kernels.cu(26): error: no operator "!" matches these operands operand types are: ! ushort4 ushort4 v__1 = !__2; ``` The same kernel compiles and returns the correct result when the loop is not vectorized (one element per thread) — so this is triggered purely by the vector width, not by the `bool` dtype itself.
Emitted CUDA for the vectorized case (width 4) — the !__2 is the crash ```cuda extern "C" __global__ void __launch_bounds__(64, 1) main_kernel(const signed char* __restrict__ A, signed char* __restrict__ C) { int __1; ushort4 __2; int v_ = *(int*)(A + (((int)threadIdx.x) * 4)); __2.x = (bool)(((char)(v_ >> 0))); __2.y = (bool)(((char)(v_ >> 8))); __2.z = (bool)(((char)(v_ >> 16))); __2.w = (bool)(((char)(v_ >> 24))); ushort4 v__1 = !__2; // <-- nvcc: no operator "!" matches ushort4 __1=((signed char)(v__1.x) << 0); ... } ``` The `bool` vector is correctly represented as a `ushort4`; only the `!` operator is un-scalarized.
Not a regression — see Provenance. ### Reproducible example code ```python import tilelang, tilelang.language as T, torch N = 256 def build(threads): @T.prim_func def main(A: T.Tensor((N,), "bool"), C: T.Tensor((N,), "bool")): with T.Kernel(1, threads=threads) as bx: for i in T.Parallel(N): # N/threads elems per thread C[i] = T.Not(A[i]) return main a = (torch.rand(N, device="cuda") > 0.5) ref = ~a # CONTROL: threads == N -> 1 elem/thread -> scalar `!x` c = tilelang.compile(build(256), out_idx=[1])(a) print("threads=256 (scalar) :", "PASS" if torch.equal(c, ref) else "FAIL") # -> PASS # REPRO: threads < N -> 4 elems/thread -> vectorized `!ushort4` c = tilelang.compile(build(64), out_idx=[1])(a) # -> nvcc compile error print("threads=64 (vector) :", "PASS" if torch.equal(c, ref) else "FAIL") ``` ### Traceback ``` tvm_kernels.cu(26): error: no operator "!" matches these operands operand types are: ! ushort4 ushort4 v__1 = !__2; ^ tvm_kernels.cu(26): note #3328-D: built-in operator!() does not match because argument #1 does not match parameter 1 error detected in the compilation of "tvm_kernels.cu". ``` ### Expected behavior The negation of a `bool` vector should compile and compute lane-by-lane, matching the scalar path (which already returns the correct result over the same inputs). Every other elementwise op in this codegen — `&&`, `||`, `+`, comparisons — already scalarizes over a vector via `PrintBinaryExpr`'s `op->dtype.lanes() == 1` split; `NotNode` is the one unary op that skips that check. ### Additional context **Root cause.** The C codegen's `NotNode` visitor does not account for a vector `dtype`, so it emits `!` against a vector operand that CUDA has no `operator!` for. In [`CodeGenC::VisitExpr_(const NotNode*)`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tvm/blob/8df8ebd61659505dd7005f4820b030e983e2c005/src/target/source/codegen_c.cc#L617) it unconditionally writes `os << '!'; PrintExpr(op->a)`, with no `lanes()` branch. Contrast [`PrintBinaryExpr`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tvm/blob/8df8ebd61659505dd7005f4820b030e983e2c005/src/target/source/codegen_c.cc#L514), which every arithmetic/logical/comparison node routes through: for `lanes() > 1` it defers to `PrintVecBinaryOp` instead of emitting a scalar operator on a vector. The CUDA codegen does not override `NotNode`, so the base-class scalar `!` reaches nvcc verbatim. **Suggested fix.** One direction is to give `NotNode` the same lane-aware handling the binary nodes have — emit a per-lane expansion (e.g. `make_ushortN(!a.x, !a.y, ...)`) when `op->dtype.lanes() > 1`, mirroring `PrintVecBinaryOp`. Whether the cleaner place is the visitor or an earlier scalarize/legalize pass is a call for the maintainers. **Class / generalization (two-level root + 4-axis sweep, all cells run on 0.1.13 / sm_89).** - **Source-level root:** `CodeGenC::VisitExpr_(const NotNode*)` at [codegen_c.cc L617](https://github.com/tile-ai/tvm/blob/8df8ebd61659505dd7005f4820b030e983e2c005/src/target/source/codegen_c.cc#L617) unconditionally emits `os << '!'; PrintExpr(op->a)` with no `op->dtype.lanes()` branch. Both binary helpers ([`PrintBinaryExpr` L514](https://github.com/tile-ai/tvm/blob/8df8ebd61659505dd7005f4820b030e983e2c005/src/target/source/codegen_c.cc#L514), `PrintBinaryIntrinsic` L536) split on `lanes()==1` and defer wide operands to `PrintVecBinaryOp`; the unary visitors do not. - **Operator-level root:** the *only* two visitor sites in `CodeGenC` that emit a C operator on a raw operand with no lane split are `NotNode` (`!`) and the `bitwise_not` intrinsic branch (`os << "(~"`, [L677](https://github.com/tile-ai/tvm/blob/8df8ebd61659505dd7005f4820b030e983e2c005/src/target/source/codegen_c.cc#L677)). Every other unary (`Cast`, and negation which is lowered to `0 - x` = a binary `SubNode`) already handles vectors. So the class boundary is exactly these two sites. | axis | cell tested (vectorized, `threads 0)`, int32→bool, width 4 | **PASS** — simplifier folds `!(x>0)` to `(x<=0)`, NotNode eliminated pre-codegen | dodges (NotNode never reaches codegen) | | related-operator | `~A[i]`, bool buffer, width 4 | `ushort4 v__1 = ~__2;` → `no operator "~" matches ... ushort4` | SIBLING site (`bitwise_not`, not `NotNode`) | | related-operator / related-type | `~A[i]`, int32, width 4 | `*(int4*)... = (~*(int4*)...)` → `no operator "~" matches ... int4` | SIBLING site (`bitwise_not`) | Takeaways: (1) the NotNode crash is width-agnostic (widths 2 and 4 both fire) and trigger-agnostic between `T.Not` and Python `not`. (2) The bug only survives when the NotNode reaches codegen — `T.Not` of a *comparison* is constant-folded by the simplifier (`!(x>0)`→`(x<=0)`) and never crashes; the defect needs a NotNode over a value the simplifier can't rewrite, e.g. a plain `bool` buffer load. (3) `~` on any buffer (bool or int) is a **distinct-but-same-root sibling** at the `bitwise_not` site, filed separately as the "vectorized `~`" issue; kept separate because they are two independent visitor sites fixable independently. Both are the single missing-`lanes()`-split pattern in `CodeGenC`. **Provenance.** The `NotNode` visitor has carried this scalar-only form in the vendored TVM `CodeGenC` (`3rdparty/tvm`, pinned at `8df8ebd6` for the 0.1.13 tag). Introduced-vs-relocated before the fork is unverified. **Dedup.** I searched the open and closed tracker and found no report of a logical-NOT crash on a vectorized `bool`. The closest are distinct mechanisms: #2206 is a `PrintType` `LogFatal` on `boolx8` (type printing, not `operator!`), and #2911/#2382 concern vector `Select`/`atomic_add` value handling. **Reach.** The trigger is first-class (`T.Not` and Python `not` over a `bool`). Auto-vectorization is the default: any `T.Parallel(N)` with `threads < N` (and `N/threads` a legal vector width) takes the vector path, so the crash fires on the common case; only `threads == extent` (one element per thread) dodges it. No shipped example negates a `bool` on the device side inside a `T.Parallel`, so CI is green. The one example that *contains* a boolean negation, `examples/block_causal_attention/block_causal_attention.py`, writes `~q_clean & ~k_clean` (line 429) only in `_dllm_mask` — a **pure-torch host-side reference** operating on `torch.Tensor`s, not device-side TileLang. Its device kernels use `int` masks with `T.if_then_else`, not `T.Not`. I ran it verbatim on 0.1.13: it compiles without the `operator!` crash (it fails only a numeric backward-gradient tolerance check, unrelated to this bug), confirming the example does **not** exercise this defect. So the "attention/masking" reach is a *plausible idiom* argument, not a shipped-example one. **Impact.** The trigger is narrow-looking (a `bool` negation whose loop happens to auto-vectorize) but sits on the default code path for the common `threads < N` case. When it fires it is a nvcc compile-time error, so it is loud and caught immediately: the kernel simply fails to build, and it cannot silently corrupt any output or slip into a running workload. Fixing it lets a legal, common idiom (elementwise negation of a boolean mask) compile in the vectorized path instead of only when one element maps to each thread; it closes a compile-time crash class, not a silent-data hazard.

title: [BUG][Fuzzer][ice-on-invalid-code] `T.gemm` on a tile with a symbolic dimension aborts with an internal `bad_optional_access` instead of clearly rejecting the unsupported symbolic tile dim
body:
### Required prerequisites - [x] I have searched the [Issue Tracker](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/issues) that this hasn't already been reported. (comment there if it has.) - [x] I have read the documentation . ### What version of TileLang are you using? 0.1.13 (latest release). ### System information Linux, TileLang 0.1.13, CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.13.0, Python 3.13, NVIDIA L40S (sm_89). The failure is at compile time (layout inference), so it is host-side and architecture-independent. ### Problem description `T.gemm` on an operand tile whose shape has a symbolic (dynamic) dimension aborts the compiler with `tvm.error.InternalError: bad_optional_access while parsing tile op call: T.gemm(...)` during `LayoutInference`. The message echoes the serialized call but does not name the offending dimension or say why it failed — it is a caught internal downcast failure, not a diagnostic. The same kernel with a static tile compiles fine. The crash comes from the `Gemm` operator's argument deserializer: it reads the tile's M/N/K as `args[i].as().value()`. When a dimension is a symbolic `tir.Var` rather than an `IntImm`, `.as()` returns an empty optional and `.value()` throws the bad-optional exception. The frontend does not reject a symbolic tile dimension before this point, so the user sees only the internal exception.
Isolating which dimension trips it Making only K symbolic (`args[7]`), only M symbolic (`args[5]`), or only N symbolic (`args[6]`), each with strides/offsets left static, reproduces the identical `bad_optional_access` — the crash is the M/N/K downcast block, not the stride/offset reads that follow it.
### Reproducible example code ```python import tilelang import tilelang.language as T M = N = 128 def build(K): @T.prim_func def main( A: T.Tensor((M, K), "float16"), B: T.Tensor((K, N), "float16"), C: T.Tensor((M, N), "float16"), ): with T.Kernel(1, 1, threads=128) as (bx, by): As = T.alloc_shared((M, K), "float16") Bs = T.alloc_shared((K, N), "float16") Cs = T.alloc_fragment((M, N), "float32") T.clear(Cs) T.copy(A, As) T.copy(B, Bs) T.gemm(As, Bs, Cs) # K is the operand-tile contraction dim T.copy(Cs, C) return main tilelang.compile(build(128), out_idx=[2]) # control: static K -> COMPILED OK tilelang.compile(build(T.symbolic("K")), out_idx=[2]) # symbolic K -> InternalError: bad_optional_access ``` ### Traceback ``` File ".../tilelang/engine/lower.py", line 289, in lower_to_host_device_ir mod = tilelang.transform.LayoutInference()(mod) File "", line 0, in tvm::tl::LayoutInferencer::Substitute(tvm::tirx::PrimFunc) ... tvm.error.InternalError: bad_optional_access while parsing tile op call: T.gemm(T.region(As[0, 0], 1, 128, K), T.region(Bs[0, 0], 1, K, 128), T.region(Cs[0, 0], 3, 128, 128), ..., 128, 128, K, ...) ``` ### Expected behavior A symbolic `T.gemm` *tile* dimension is genuinely unsupported, so the right outcome is a clear rejection, not an internal crash. The tile M/N/K must be compile-time constants for this code path to work at all: the tensor-core instruction selection (which MMA/WGMMA shape, how many issues), the operand fragment layout inference, and the K-loop unrolling all consume the static tile extents — a symbolic tile dim has no MMA to select and no fragment layout to infer. (This is distinct from dynamic *global* shapes, which TileLang does support: a runtime `M_total` is fine as a grid/loop bound; only the per-block tile extent must be static.) So the fix is a compile-time diagnostic that names the operation and the offending dimension — e.g. `T.gemm requires static tile dimensions, but got a symbolic K` — instead of the internal `bad_optional_access`. TileLang already treats a symbolic extent reaching an unchecked `.as()` as a bug elsewhere (#2906, `makeBufferWithLayout`), where the fix direction is the guard/diagnostic that was intended but never fired; the same framing applies here. (If dynamic-tile GEMM were ever intended, that is a much larger feature — runtime instruction selection — not this defect.) ### Additional context **Root cause.** The `Gemm` operator's argument deserializer assumes the M/N/K tile dimensions are compile-time constants and downcasts them unconditionally with `.as().value()`; a symbolic dimension makes that optional empty and `.value()` throws. In [`src/op/gemm.cc#L99-L101`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/src/op/gemm.cc#L99-L101): ```cpp node->m_ = args[5].as().value()->value; node->n_ = args[6].as().value()->value; node->k_ = args[7].as().value()->value; ``` The immediately-following [`clear_accum` argument](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/src/op/gemm.cc#L103) is read with `.as()`, which accepts a symbolic value — so this same constructor already handles non-constant arguments for one field but not for M/N/K. On the frontend side, M/N/K are taken straight from the operand/tile shapes with no static-shape check ([`gemm_op.py#L77-L89`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/tilelang/language/gemm_op.py#L77-L89)), so a symbolic tile dimension flows through to the constructor unguarded. **Suggested fix.** Check each of M/N/K for `IntImm` (frontend or constructor) and raise a clear error naming `T.gemm` and the symbolic dimension when it isn't constant — a static-tile requirement that MMA atom/warp-partition selection already needs. **Provenance.** The M/N/K `.as().value()` reads are present in the `Gemm` serialized-argument constructor at the 0.1.13 release (also present in 0.1.9); I did not pin the introducing PR. Not established as a regression. **Dedup.** I searched the open and closed tracker and found no existing report of the `T.gemm` symbolic-tile-dimension crash. Distinct from #2906 (`makeBufferWithLayout` SIGSEGV on a symbolic shared-buffer extent): same theme (a symbolic extent reaching an unchecked `IntImm` downcast) but a different site (`lower_tile_op.cc` vs the `Gemm` constructor), different trigger (requires a `T.annotate_layout`; this needs only `T.gemm`), and a different symptom (SIGSEGV vs a caught `InternalError`). **Tested boundary (input family).** Cells run on 0.1.13/L40S, one symbolic tile dim at a time: symbolic `K` (`args[7]`), symbolic `M` (`args[5]`), and symbolic `N` (`args[6]`) each abort with the identical `bad_optional_access`; the fully-static control compiles. The dtype is irrelevant — an `int8`×`int8`→`int32` GEMM with symbolic `K` aborts identically. All share one root — the unconditional `.as().value()` on `args[5..7]` — so this is one missing-guard class over the M/N/K downcast block, not three adjacent bugs. **Reach.** The trigger is a documented construct (`T.dynamic`/`T.symbolic`, TileLang's dynamic-shape API) used *directly* as a `T.gemm` operand-tile dimension. Dynamic shapes are common in the shipped examples — 52 files under `examples/`+`testing/` use `T.symbolic`/`T.dynamic` at 0.1.13, ~25 of them alongside `T.gemm` — but the dynamic dimension is always the *global* tensor extent, while the GEMM operand tiles are allocated with static `block_M/N/K`. I ran the dedicated [`examples/dynamic_shape/example_dynamic.py`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/examples/dynamic_shape/example_dynamic.py) **verbatim at its default config** (M=N=K=16384, block 128/128/32) on 0.1.13/L40S: it compiles, matches the torch reference (`Kernel output matches PyTorch reference.`), and benchmarks (`Latency: 154.26 ms`) — it does **not** trip the crash. It dodges because its `T.gemm(A_shared, B_shared, C_local, ...)` operand tiles are `alloc_shared((block_M, block_K), ...)` etc. with static `block_*`; the symbolic `m/n/k` only size the *global* `A/B/C` tensors and the grid. I confirmed this boundary directly: a kernel with a symbolic *global* extent `M` but a static GEMM tile (the example's pattern) compiles OK — the crash requires the symbolic value to reach a GEMM operand-tile M/N/K, which no shipped example does. This is why CI is green. **Generalization (§17).** Two-level root: - **Source-level root (fragile impl):** the `Gemm` serialized-argument constructor in [`src/op/gemm.cc#L99-L101`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/src/op/gemm.cc#L99-L101) reads the tile M/N/K with an unconditional `args[i].as().value()->value`. The optional is empty for a symbolic `tir.Var`, and `.value()` throws the caught `bad_optional_access` during `LayoutInference`. The frontend ([`gemm_op.py#L77-L89`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/tilelang/language/gemm_op.py#L77-L89)) reads M/N/K straight from operand shapes with no static-shape check, so a symbolic tile dim flows through unguarded. - **Operator-level root:** any tile-op constructor that downcasts a *buffer-derived tile shape* via `.as().value()` without first checking it is constant. **4-axis sweep** (all cells run on 0.1.13/L40S, fresh process + cache each): | Axis | Cell tested | Observed result | Same-root? | |---|---|---|---| | input-family (dim) | `T.gemm` symbolic `M` (args[5]) | `InternalError bad_optional_access` | yes — same M/N/K block | | input-family (dim) | `T.gemm` symbolic `N` (args[6]) | `InternalError bad_optional_access` | yes | | related-type (dtype) | `int8×int8→int32` `T.gemm`, symbolic `K` | `InternalError bad_optional_access` | yes — downcast is on shape, dtype-independent | | related-operator | `T.gemm_sp` (sparse), symbolic operand `Kc` | `InternalError bad_optional_access` (identical, `T.gemm_sp(...)` echoed) | **yes** — [`gemm_sp.cc#L110-L112`](https://github.com/tile-ai/tilelang/blob/8001cc4ccf6149382d2019654a19f59c1d4d0482/src/op/gemm_sp.cc#L110-L112) has the identical M/N/K `.as().value()` idiom | | similar-logic (boundary) | symbolic *global* extent `M`, static GEMM tile | `COMPILED OK (no crash)` | boundary — does NOT fire; explains why examples dodge | | related-source (distinct) | `reduce.cc:82` / `scan.cc:65` `dim`, `copy.cc:589-593` conv attrs | not run — argument is a compile-time-only attribute (reduction axis / conv kernel/stride/pad), never a buffer-derived symbolic shape | distinct trigger, same code idiom | **Reframe decision.** The class spans two operators (`T.gemm` and `T.gemm_sp`) that share the identical constructor idiom and produce the identical crash. But `T.gemm_sp` needs Hopper (WGMMA/tcgen05) sparse metadata and a sparse workflow that no user hits casually, whereas `T.gemm` is the common path — and the sparse frontend's own structural K-check (`2*(K//2) == K`) blocks the naive symbolic-K spelling first (a separate syntactic-guard weakness). I keep the issue titled and scoped to `T.gemm` for a minimal, common repro, and record `T.gemm_sp` here as a **same-root sibling** the fix should cover (guard M/N/K in both constructors, or in a shared helper).
